Always, since family loans fall outside FINRA rules entirely
Only if the loan carries interest at or above the prime rate

explanation: FINRA prohibits reps from borrowing from or lending to customers unless the firm has written procedures allowing it and the arrangement fits a permitted category, such as an immediate family member or a lending institution. Some categories also need notice to or approval from the firm.

distractorExplanations.a: FINRA allows some loans, for example from immediate family, if the firm's written procedures permit them.

prompt: A rep wants to share in the profits and losses of a customer's account. The customer is not a family member. What is required?

options.text: A signed guarantee that the rep will cover any losses in full
Written approval from firm and customer, shared in proportion
Approval from FINRA, with any agreed profit split then allowed
Nothing, if the customer agrees to the arrangement verbally

explanation: A rep may share in a customer account only with prior written approval from the firm and the customer, and only in proportion to the rep's own contribution to the account. Accounts with immediate family members are excepted from the proportion rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Guaranteeing customers against loss is prohibited, so it cannot be a condition for sharing.
distractorExplanations.c: Approval comes from the firm and the customer, not FINRA, and the sharing must be proportionate to the rep's contribution.
distractorExplanations.d: Verbal agreement is not enough; both the firm and the customer must approve the arrangement in writing.

prompt: How often must a broker-dealer send account statements to a customer whose account has activity?

options.text: Only when the customer asks for one in writing
Only once a year, at the end of the tax year
After every trade, in place of a confirmation
At least once each calendar quarter

explanation: FINRA requires member firms to send customer account statements at least quarterly, showing positions, balances and activity. Many firms send them monthly when there is activity.

distractorExplanations.a: Statements are mandatory; the firm cannot wait for a request.
distractorExplanations.b: Annual statements do not meet FINRA's requirement; statements must be sent at least quarterly.
distractorExplanations.c: Confirmations are sent for each trade, but they do not replace periodic account statements.

prompt: A customer gives her son a limited power of attorney over her brokerage account. What can the son do?

options.text: Change the account's beneficiaries and its owner
Enter trades, but not withdraw cash or securities
Close the account and open a new one in his own name
Withdraw cash and securities to his own account

explanation: A limited power of attorney (limited trading authorization) lets the agent buy and sell in the account but not withdraw assets. A full power of attorney also allows withdrawals and other changes.

distractorExplanations.a: Changing ownership or beneficiaries is beyond a limited trading authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: A limited power of attorney does not allow changing ownership or closing the account.
distractorExplanations.d: That needs a full power of attorney; limited authority covers trading only.

prompt: A rep learns that a customer with an individual account has died. What should the firm do first?

options.text: Sell all positions to cash so the value cannot fall further
Keep the open orders working until the executor gives instructions
Transfer the assets to the customer's spouse at once
Cancel open orders and freeze the account until documents arrive

explanation: On notice of the death of a sole account owner, the firm cancels open orders, freezes the account and waits for documents such as a death certificate and letters testamentary appointing the executor, who then gives instructions.

distractorExplanations.a: No one has authority to trade until the executor is appointed; selling without instructions is not allowed.
distractorExplanations.b: Open orders must be canceled on notice of death, since the dead owner can no longer give instructions.
distractorExplanations.c: Assets in an individual account pass through the estate, so the firm needs the executor's documents first.

prompt: FINRA's suitability rule includes three obligations. Which one is breached when a rep's trades are each suitable alone but excessive in number for the customer?

options.text: Best execution
Reasonable-basis suitability
Customer-specific suitability
Quantitative suitability

explanation: Suitability has three parts: reasonable-basis (the product is suitable for some investors), customer-specific (it fits this customer), and quantitative (the series of trades is not excessive). Excessive trading, as in churning, breaches quantitative suitability.

distractorExplanations.a: Best execution is about getting the most favorable terms for an order, not how often the rep trades.
distractorExplanations.b: Reasonable-basis is about understanding a product well enough to recommend it to anyone; the issue here is trading frequency.
distractorExplanations.c: Customer-specific is about whether one recommendation fits the customer's profile; the problem is the number of trades.

prompt: A customer's shares are held in street name at her broker-dealer. The company holds a shareholder vote. How does she receive the proxy materials?

options.text: She receives nothing, since the firm votes the shares
The company mails them only to the transfer agent
She must first move the shares into her own registered name
The firm forwards them to her as the beneficial owner

explanation: In street name, the firm is the registered owner but the customer is the beneficial owner. The firm must pass proxy materials and annual reports to her so she can vote her shares.

distractorExplanations.a: The customer is the beneficial owner and is entitled to the proxy materials and to vote.
distractorExplanations.b: The transfer agent keeps records; proxy materials must reach the beneficial owner through the firm.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding in street name does not remove her right to vote; the firm passes the materials to her.

prompt: A stock is quoted at $20.10 bid and $20.15 ask. A customer places a market order to buy. At about what price will the order fill?

options.text: $20.05, the last trade price
$20.10, the bid
$20.125, the midpoint of the spread
$20.15, the ask

explanation: The bid is the highest price buyers will pay and the ask (offer) is the lowest price sellers will accept. A customer buying at market pays the ask; a customer selling at market receives the bid.

distractorExplanations.a: The last sale is history; a new market buy order fills at the current ask.
distractorExplanations.b: The bid is what buyers pay a seller; a customer buying at market pays the ask.
distractorExplanations.c: A market order does not usually fill at the midpoint; buyers pay the offer price.

prompt: A customer sold short 200 shares of a stock that then pays a $0.50 cash dividend. What happens?

options.text: She receives $100, the dividend on the 200 shares
She must pay $100 to the lender of the shares
Nothing happens, because she does not own the shares
The firm pays the dividend to the company on her behalf

explanation: A short seller borrowed the shares, so the lender is still entitled to dividends. The short seller's account is charged the dividend, here 200 × $0.50 = $100.

distractorExplanations.a: The short seller does not own the shares; the lender is entitled to the dividend.
distractorExplanations.c: She must make the lender whole, so she pays the dividend amount.
distractorExplanations.d: Dividends go from the company to shareholders; the short seller pays the lender, not the company.

prompt: A margin account holds stock with a market value of $20,000 and a debit balance of $12,000. What is the customer's equity?
explanation: Equity in a long margin account = market value − debit balance = $20,000 − $12,000 = $8,000. This is 40% of market value, above the 25% FINRA maintenance minimum.

distractorExplanations.b: That is the debit balance, the amount borrowed, not the customer's equity.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the market value; equity is what remains after subtracting the debit balance.
distractorExplanations.d: Adds the debit to market value instead of subtracting it.

prompt: A customer deposits $12,000 in cash at once to buy securities. What must the broker-dealer file?

options.text: A Suspicious Activity Report, since all cash is suspicious
Nothing, since cash deposits are not reported
A Currency Transaction Report with FinCEN
A Form U5 with FINRA

explanation: Firms must file a Currency Transaction Report with FinCEN for cash transactions over $10,000 in one business day. Breaking deposits into smaller amounts to avoid this is structuring, which can lead to a SAR.

distractorExplanations.a: A SAR is filed when activity is suspicious, not for every cash deposit; the CTR is required for cash over $10,000.
distractorExplanations.b: Cash over $10,000 in one business day triggers a Currency Transaction Report.
distractorExplanations.d: Form U5 is filed when a registered person leaves a firm; it has nothing to do with cash deposits.

prompt: A rep urges customers to buy a stock right before its ex-dividend date, saying they will 'get the dividend for free.' What is wrong with this?

options.text: It is churning, since the rep is trading the account too often
It is front running, since the rep traded ahead of customers
Nothing, since the customers do receive the dividend
It is selling dividends, a prohibited practice

explanation: Selling dividends means pushing customers to buy just before the ex-date to capture a dividend. The price drops by about the dividend amount on the ex-date, and the dividend is taxable, so the customer gains nothing and may pay more tax.

distractorExplanations.a: Churning is excessive trading for commissions; this misrepresents the value of a dividend.
distractorExplanations.b: Front running involves trading ahead of a customer order; here the rep is misleading customers about dividends.
distractorExplanations.c: The share price falls by about the dividend on the ex-date, and the dividend is taxable, so there is no free gain.

prompt: A customer plans to invest $48,000 in a fund that offers a reduced sales charge at $50,000. The rep does not mention the breakpoint. What is the concern?

options.text: Nothing, since disclosing breakpoints is optional
Front running, since the rep acted ahead of the fund
Breakpoint selling, a prohibited practice
Market manipulation, since the fund price was moved

explanation: Breakpoint selling means selling just below a breakpoint, or failing to tell a customer that a little more money would lower the sales charge. It is prohibited because the customer pays a higher load and the rep earns more.

distractorExplanations.a: Firms must tell customers about breakpoints; failing to do so to earn a higher sales charge is prohibited.
distractorExplanations.b: Front running involves trading ahead of a customer's order, not failing to mention a breakpoint.
distractorExplanations.d: Nothing moved the fund's price; the issue is that the customer paid a higher sales charge than needed.

prompt: A customer tells a rep, 'Buy a tech stock you like this afternoon; spend up to $10,000.' The account has no discretionary authority. What may the rep do?

options.text: Place the trade, because the customer chose the amount to spend
Place the trade, because it will be completed the same day
Decline, since choosing the security needs written authority
Place the trade, then send the customer a written confirmation afterward

explanation: Discretion means the rep chooses the asset, the amount or the action (buy or sell). It requires the customer's prior written authorization and principal approval. Same-day time and price discretion is the only exception.

distractorExplanations.a: Choosing which security to buy is discretion; it needs written authorization, even if the customer set the amount.
distractorExplanations.b: The same-day exception covers only time and price, not choosing the security.
distractorExplanations.d: A confirmation does not cure an unauthorized discretionary trade.
